[Lesson 11]{.custom-subtitle} [*Neural Networks*]{.custom-subtitle} --- ## {#in-this-lesson data-menu-title="In this lesson"} [In this lesson]{.slide-title}

- A brief history of neural networks and why they are relevant today - The structure of a single-layer neural network: input layer, hidden layer, and output layer - How activations are computed and what activation functions do - Multilayer (deep) neural networks and how they extend the single-layer idea - Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for image data --- ## {#section-history data-menu-title="# Neural network applications #" background="#047C90"}

Neural network applications

--- ## {#nn-history data-menu-title="A brief history"} [A brief history]{.slide-title}
- **Early excitement**: neural networks appeared early in the history of machine learning (going back to the 1960s), generating significant enthusiasm . . . - **Decline**: interest waned as other methods — SVMs, random forests — outperformed them, especially on structured tabular data . . . - **The 2010s revival**: two forces brought them back: - *New architectures* (deep networks with many hidden layers) - *Massive datasets* that made training those architectures feasible . . . ::: {.center-text .teal-text .body-text-m} This resurgence is what we now call **deep learning** ::: --- ## {#nn-applications data-menu-title="Applications"} [Applications]{.slide-title}
Deep neural networks are at the heart of many contemporary technological advancements:
- **Large language models**: used for text and code generation (ChatGPT, Claude) — neural networks with likely *trillions* of parameters - **Image recognition**: identifying objects in images, with applications from autonomous vehicles to medical imaging . . .
::: {.body-text-m} In the realm of **environmental applications**: - [Yu et al. 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-60091-y): inequities in EV charging station access for disadvantaged communities - [Wunsch et al. 2022](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-022-28770-2): projected groundwater levels under climate change - [Hopkinson et al. 2020](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0230671): classifying coral reef 3D models into species and substrates ::: --- ## {#section-single data-menu-title="# Single-layer neural network #" background="#047C90"}

Single-layer neural network

--- ## {#nn-setup data-menu-title="Setup"} [Setup]{.slide-title}
Given a vector of features $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \ldots, X_p)$ and a response variable $Y$, our goal is to learn a function $F(\mathbf{X})$ to predict $Y$ — same goal as throughout the course. . . .
A **single-layer neural network** (a network with one hidden layer) has three core components:
::: {.body-text-m} 1. **Input layer** — the $p$ features $X_1, \ldots, X_p$ 2. **Hidden layer** — $K$ **neurons**, each computing an **activation** 3. **Output layer** — the final model output $F(\mathbf{X})$ ::: --- ## {#nn-diagram-slide data-menu-title="Architecture diagram"} [Architecture]{.slide-title}
::: {#cell-nn-diagram-slides .cell execution_count=2} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](11_neural_networks-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/nn-diagram-slides-output-1.png){#nn-diagram-slides width=867 height=585 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#nn-process data-menu-title="The process"} [The process]{.slide-title}
::: {.body-text-m} **Step 1 — Input layer.** An observation $(X_1, \ldots, X_p)$ is fed through the network left to right. . . . **Step 2 — Hidden layer.** Each neuron $k$ computes an activation $A_k$ in two steps: - Form a linear combination using a **bias** $w_{k0}$ and **weights** $w_{k1}, \ldots, w_{kp}$: $$w_{k0} + w_{k1} X_1 + \cdots + w_{kp} X_p$$ - Pass through a nonlinear **activation function** $g(z)$: $$A_k = g(w_{k0} + w_{k1} X_1 + \cdots + w_{kp} X_p)$$ Each neuron has $p + 1$ parameters ($p$ weights + 1 bias). . . . **Step 3 — Output layer.** Final prediction is a linear combination of all $K$ activations: $$F(X_1, \ldots, X_p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 A_1 + \cdots + \beta_K A_K$$ ::: --- ## {#nn-fitting data-menu-title="Fitting"} [Fitting a neural network]{.slide-title}
Fitting means estimating all weights $w_{kj}$, biases $w_{k0}$, and output coefficients $\beta_0, \ldots, \beta_K$ from the training data. . . .
We minimize a **loss function** that measures prediction error: - **Regression**: mean squared error - **Classification**: [cross-entropy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross-entropy) . . .
This is done via **stochastic gradient descent** + **backpropagation**, which efficiently computes gradients of the loss with respect to every parameter. ::: {.body-text-s .center-text} *(See ISLP §10.7 for details on the fitting algorithm)* ::: --- ## {#section-activations data-menu-title="# Activation functions #" background="#047C90"}

Activation functions

--- ## {#activation-intro data-menu-title="Why activation functions?"} [Why activation functions?]{.slide-title}
The activation function introduces the **nonlinearity** that gives neural networks their modeling power. . . .
::: {.center-text .teal-text .body-text-m} Without it, the entire network would collapse to a **linear model** — regardless of how many layers it has. ::: . . .
Two of the most common choices: ::: {.body-text-m} - **Sigmoid**: $\displaystyle g(z) = \frac{e^z}{1 + e^z}$ — squashes any input to $(0, 1)$ - **ReLU** (Rectified Linear Unit): $g(z) = \max(0, z)$ — zero for negative inputs, identity for positive ::: --- ## {#activation-plot data-menu-title="Activation functions"} [Activation functions]{.slide-title}
::: {#cell-activation-functions-slides .cell execution_count=3} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](11_neural_networks-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/activation-functions-slides-output-1.png){#activation-functions-slides width=1104 height=434 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#section-multilayer data-menu-title="# Multilayer neural networks #" background="#047C90"}

Multilayer neural networks

--- ## {#multilayer-intro data-menu-title="Multilayer neural networks"} [Multilayer neural networks]{.slide-title}
In practice, neural networks have **more than one hidden layer** and many neurons per layer (often hundreds). This is what makes them *deep* networks. . . .
**First hidden layer** ($K_1$ neurons): $$\begin{aligned} A_k^{(1)} &= g\!\left(w_{k0}^{(1)} + w_{k1}^{(1)} X_1 + \cdots + w_{kp}^{(1)} X_p\right) \\ &= g\!\left(w_{k0}^{(1)} + \sum_{j=1}^{p} w_{kj}^{(1)} X_j\right) \end{aligned}$$ . . . **Second hidden layer** ($K_2$ neurons) — takes the previous layer's activations as input: $$\begin{aligned} A_k^{(2)} &= g\!\left(w_{k0}^{(2)} + w_{k1}^{(2)} A_1^{(1)} + \cdots + w_{kK_1}^{(2)} A_{K_1}^{(1)}\right) \\ &= g\!\left(w_{k0}^{(2)} + \sum_{j=1}^{K_1} w_{kj}^{(2)} A_j^{(1)}\right) \end{aligned}$$ --- ## {#multilayer-diagram-slide data-menu-title="Multilayer architecture diagram"} [Multilayer architecture]{.slide-title}
::: {#cell-multilayer-nn-diagram-slides .cell execution_count=4} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](11_neural_networks-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/multilayer-nn-diagram-slides-output-1.png){#multilayer-nn-diagram-slides width=1027 height=585 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#multilayer-depth data-menu-title="Depth and representations"} [Depth and representations]{.slide-title}
As the network grows deeper, it can represent increasingly complex functions.
::: {.body-text-m} - **Early layers** tend to capture simple, low-level patterns - **Deeper layers** combine them into progressively abstract representations ::: . . .
To build an intuitive understanding of how deep networks work, watch: ::: {.center-text .body-text-m} [3Blue1Brown — *But what is a neural network?*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aircAruvnKk) ::: ::: {.body-text-s} As you watch, think about: 1. How does the network represent a handwritten digit as an input? 2. What does each neuron in a hidden layer conceptually "detect"? 3. Why can depth capture more complex patterns than a single very wide layer? ::: --- ## {#section-cnn data-menu-title="# Convolutional neural networks #" background="#047C90"}

Convolutional neural networks

--- ## {#cnn-motivation data-menu-title="CNNs: motivation"} [Convolutional neural networks]{.slide-title}
The networks we have studied treat the input as a **flat vector of features** — this discards spatial structure when the input is an image. . . .
**CNNs** are designed specifically for image data: ::: {.body-text-m} - Rather than connecting every input to every neuron, CNNs first identify **low-level features** — small edges, patches of color, textures - These are combined into **higher-level features** (shapes, objects, patterns) in later layers - The presence of high-level features determines the predicted class ::: . . .
::: {.center-text .teal-text} In environmental science: land cover classification, deforestation detection, species identification in camera traps ::: --- ## {#convolution-filter data-menu-title="Convolution filters"} [Convolution filters]{.slide-title}
A **convolution filter** (kernel) is a small matrix that acts as a feature detector. We slide it across the image, computing a dot product at each position → **feature map**. ::: {#cell-convolution-example-slides .cell execution_count=5} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](11_neural_networks-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/convolution-example-slides-output-1.png){#convolution-example-slides width=1015 height=385 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ::: {.body-text-s .center-text} Higher values (darker green) = region closely resembles the filter. Filters are **learned from training data** — the network discovers the most useful features automatically. ::: --- ## {#pooling-slide data-menu-title="Pooling layer"} [Pooling layer]{.slide-title}
A **pooling layer** reduces the spatial size of feature maps — more compact and less sensitive to small shifts in feature position. **Max pooling**: divide into non-overlapping blocks, retain only the **maximum** value per block. ::: {#cell-max-pooling-slides .cell execution_count=6} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](11_neural_networks-SLIDES_files/figure-revealjs/max-pooling-slides-output-1.png){#max-pooling-slides width=547 height=326 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: --- ## {#full-cnn data-menu-title="Full CNN architecture"} [Full CNN architecture]{.slide-title}
A complete CNN combines: ::: {.body-text-m} 1. **Convolution layers** — learn low-level features (edges, textures, patches of color) 2. **Pooling layers** — progressively reduce spatial dimensions 3. **Flattening** — convert final feature maps into a flat vector 4. **Fully connected layers** — combine high-level features to produce the final prediction :::
